newsitem.title: USA: Labor board to appeal on behalf of Detroit strikers.
newsitem.headline: Labor board to appeal on behalf of Detroit strikers.

text.p: A U.S. labor group said on Friday it will appeal a federal judge's refusal to order Detroit's two newspapers to immediately take back more than 1,000 strikers who walked off the job more than two years ago.

The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) had asked U.S. District Court Judge John Corbett O'Meara for a preliminary injunction that would force the Detroit Free Press and Detroit News to put the strikers back to work.
"After carefully reviewing the judge's opinion, I continue to believe we have a strong case and that the judge erred in failing to give the requested injunctive relief," the NLRB said in a statement.
The labor group expects to file an appeal in the next few weeks and union members remained optimistic.
"We are disappointed. But this is a set back, not a defeat," said Alfred Derey, chair of the some 2,000 strong Metropolitan Council of Newspaper Unions.
"(The decision) failed to recognize the well-established legal rights of our people."
About 2,500 distribution, editorial and production workers represented by six unions walked off the job July 13, 1995, when contract talks collapsed.

In June, an administrative law judge agreed with the strikers that the papers and their joint operating agency had committed unfair labor practices. He also ordered the papers to reinstate all unfair labor practice strikers, even if it means displacing workers hired since the strike.

When the papers appealed the decision, the NLRB asked for a federal court order. The NLRB argued that by the time the lengthy appeals process is over, strikers would be gone and the collective bargaining process would be harmed.

But the papers said the judge should not interfere with the legal process. In his ruling, O'Meara said it would be premature to grant the injunction while the unfair labor practice issues work their way through the legal system, said Susie Ellwood, a spokeswoman for Detroit Newspapers Inc., which operates the two papers.
However, the NLRB said: "I believe that the record facts demonstrate that an injunction is necessary to preserve the integrity of the bargaining process."
The Detroit Free Press is owned by Knight-Ridder Co.. Gannett Co Inc. owns the Detroit News. The papers are editorially independent but jointly published through Detroit Newspapers.
